1 --- 2 title: Linking and Navigating 3 description: Learn how the built-in navigation optimizations work, including prefetching, prerendering, and client-side navigation, and how to optimize navigation for dynamic routes and slow networks. 4 related: 5 links: 6 - app/api-reference/components/link 7 - app/api-reference/file-conventions/loading 8 - app/guides/prefetching 9 --- 10 11 In Next.js, routes are rendered on the server by default. This often means the client has to wait for a server response before a new route can be shown. Next.js comes with built-in [prefetching](#prefetching), [streaming](#streaming), and [client-side transitions](#client-side-transitions) ensuring navigation stays fast and responsive. 12 13 This guide explains how navigation works in Next.js and how you can optimize it for [dynamic routes](#dynamic-routes-without-loadingtsx) and [slow networks](#slow-networks). 14 15 ## How navigation works 16 17 To understand how navigation works in Next.js, it helps to be familiar with the following concepts: 18 19 - [Server Rendering](#server-rendering) 20 - [Prefetching](#prefetching) 21 - [Streaming](#streaming) 22 - [Client-side transitions](#client-side-transitions) 23 24 ### Server Rendering 25 26 In Next.js, [Layouts and Pages](/docs/app/getting-started/layouts-and-pages) are [React Server Components](https://react.dev/reference/rsc/server-components) by default. On initial and subsequent navigations, the [Server Component Payload](/docs/app/getting-started/server-and-client-components#how-do-server-and-client-components-work-in-nextjs) is generated on the server before being sent to the client. 27 28 There are two types of server rendering, based on _when_ it happens: 29 30 - **Prerendering** happens at build time or during [revalidation](/docs/app/getting-started/revalidating) and the result is cached. 31 - **Dynamic Rendering** happens at request time in response to a client request. 32 33 The trade-off of server rendering is that the client must wait for the server to respond before the new route can be shown. Next.js addresses this delay by [prefetching](#prefetching) routes the user is likely to visit and performing [client-side transitions](#client-side-transitions). 34 35 > **Good to know**: HTML is also generated for the initial visit. 36 37 ### Prefetching 38 39 Prefetching is the process of loading a route in the background before the user navigates to it. This makes navigation between routes in your application feel instant, because by the time a user clicks on a link, the data to render the next route is already available client side. 40 41 Next.js automatically prefetches routes linked with the [`` component](/docs/app/api-reference/components/link) when they enter the user's viewport. 42 43 ```tsx filename="app/layout.tsx" switcher 44 import Link from 'next/link' 45 46 export default function Layout({ children }: { children: React.ReactNode }) { 47 return ( 48 49 50
51 {/* Prefetched when the link is hovered or enters the viewport */} 52 Blog 53 {/* No prefetching */} 54 Contact 55
56 {children} 57 58 59 ) 60 } 61 ``` 62 63 ```jsx filename="app/layout.js" switcher 64 import Link from 'next/link' 65 66 export default function Layout({ children }) { 67 return ( 68 69 70
71 {/* Prefetched when the link is hovered or enters the viewport */} 72 Blog 73 {/* No prefetching */} 74 Contact 75
76 {children} 77 78 79 ) 80 } 81 ``` 82 83 How much of the route is prefetched depends on whether it's static or dynamic: 84 85 - **Static Route**: the full route is prefetched. 86 - **Dynamic Route**: prefetching is skipped, or the route is partially prefetched if [`loading.tsx`](/docs/app/api-reference/file-conventions/loading) is present. 87 88 By skipping or partially prefetching dynamic routes, Next.js avoids unnecessary work on the server for routes the users may never visit. However, waiting for a server response before navigation can give the users the impression that the app is not responding. 89 90 97 98 > **Good to know:** See the [Prefetching guide](/docs/app/guides/prefetching) for the full behavior, including how to control prefetching per link and how it changes when you adopt [Partial Prefetching](/docs/app/guides/adopting-partial-prefetching). 99 100 To improve the navigation experience to dynamic routes, you can use [streaming](#streaming). 101 102 ### Streaming 103 104 Streaming allows the server to send parts of a dynamic route to the client as soon as they're ready, rather than waiting for the entire route to be rendered. This means users see something sooner, even if parts of the page are still loading. See the [Streaming guide](/docs/app/guides/streaming) for a deep dive into how streaming works in Next.js. 105 106 For dynamic routes, it means they can be **partially prefetched**. That is, shared layouts and loading skeletons can be requested ahead of time. 107 108 115 116 To use streaming, create a `loading.tsx` in your route folder: 117 118 125 126 ```tsx filename="app/dashboard/loading.tsx" switcher 127 export default function Loading() { 128 // Add fallback UI that will be shown while the route is loading. 129 return 130 } 131 ``` 132 133 ```jsx filename="app/dashboard/loading.js" switcher 134 export default function Loading() { 135 // Add fallback UI that will be shown while the route is loading. 136 return 137 } 138 ``` 139 140 Behind the scenes, Next.js will automatically wrap the `page.tsx` contents in a `` boundary. The prefetched fallback UI will be shown while the route is loading, and swapped for the actual content once ready. 141 142 > **Good to know**: You can also use [``](https://react.dev/reference/react/Suspense) to create loading UI for nested components. 143 144 Benefits of `loading.tsx`: 145 146 - Immediate navigation and visual feedback for the user. 147 - Shared layouts remain interactive and navigation is interruptible. 148 - Improved Core Web Vitals: [TTFB](https://web.dev/articles/ttfb), [FCP](https://web.dev/articles/fcp), and [TTI](https://web.dev/articles/tti). 149 150 To further improve the navigation experience, Next.js performs a [client-side transition](#client-side-transitions) with the `` component. 151 152 ### Client-side transitions 153 154 Traditionally, navigation to a server-rendered page triggers a full page load. This clears state, resets scroll position, and blocks interactivity. 155 156 Next.js avoids this with client-side transitions using the `` component. Instead of reloading the page, it updates the content dynamically by: 157 158 - Keeping any shared layouts and UI. 159 - Replacing the current page with the prefetched loading state or a new page if available. 160 161 Client-side transitions are what makes a server-rendered apps _feel_ like client-rendered apps. And when paired with [prefetching](#prefetching) and [streaming](#streaming), it enables fast transitions, even for dynamic routes. 162 163 Next.js also handles [scrolling to the top of the page](/docs/app/api-reference/components/link#scroll) during client-side transitions. If content scrolls behind a sticky or fixed header after navigation, you can fix this with CSS [`scroll-padding-top`](/docs/app/api-reference/components/link#scroll-offset-with-sticky-headers). 164 165 ## What can make transitions slow? 166 167 These Next.js optimizations make navigation fast and responsive. However, under certain conditions, transitions can still _feel_ slow. Here are some common causes and how to improve the user experience: 168 169 ### Dynamic routes without `loading.tsx` 170 171 When navigating to a dynamic route, the client must wait for the server response before showing the result. This can give the users the impression that the app is not responding. 172 173 We recommend adding `loading.tsx` to dynamic routes to enable partial prefetching, trigger immediate navigation, and display a loading UI while the route renders. 174 175 ```tsx filename="app/blog/[slug]/loading.tsx" switcher 176 export default function Loading() { 177 return 178 } 179 ``` 180 181 ```jsx filename="app/blog/[slug]/loading.js" switcher 182 export default function Loading() { 183 return 184 } 185 ``` 186 187 > **Good to know**: In development mode, you can use the Next.js Devtools to identify if the route is static or dynamic. See [`devIndicators`](/docs/app/api-reference/config/next-config-js/devIndicators) for more information. 188 189 ### Dynamic segments without `generateStaticParams` 190 191 If a [dynamic segment](/docs/app/api-reference/file-conventions/dynamic-routes) could be prerendered but isn't because it's missing [`generateStaticParams`](/docs/app/api-reference/functions/generate-static-params), the route will fallback to dynamic rendering at request time. 192 193 Ensure the route is statically generated at build time by adding `generateStaticParams`: 194 195 ```tsx filename="app/blog/[slug]/page.tsx" switcher 196 export async function generateStaticParams() { 197 const posts = await fetch('https://.../posts').then((res) => res.json()) 198 199 return posts.map((post) => ({ 200 slug: post.slug, 201 })) 202 } 203 204 export default async function Page({ 205 params, 206 }: { 207 params: Promise<{ slug: string }> 208 }) { 209 const { slug } = await params 210 // ... 211 } 212 ``` 213 214 ```jsx filename="app/blog/[slug]/page.js" switcher 215 export async function generateStaticParams() { 216 const posts = await fetch('https://.../posts').then((res) => res.json()) 217 218 return posts.map((post) => ({ 219 slug: post.slug, 220 })) 221 } 222 223 export default async function Page({ params }) { 224 const { slug } = await params 225 // ... 226 } 227 ``` 228 229 ### Slow networks 230 231 On slow or unstable networks, prefetching may not finish before the user clicks a link. This can affect both static and dynamic routes. In these cases, the `loading.js` fallback may not appear immediately because it hasn't been prefetched yet. 232 233 To improve perceived performance, you can use the [`useLinkStatus` hook](/docs/app/api-reference/functions/use-link-status) to show immediate feedback while the transition is in progress. 234 235 ```tsx filename="app/ui/loading-indicator.tsx" switcher 236 'use client' 237 238 import { useLinkStatus } from 'next/link' 239 240 export default function LoadingIndicator() { 241 const { pending } = useLinkStatus() 242 return ( 243 244 ) 245 } 246 ``` 247 248 ```jsx filename="app/ui/loading-indicator.js" switcher 249 'use client' 250 251 import { useLinkStatus } from 'next/link' 252 253 export default function LoadingIndicator() { 254 const { pending } = useLinkStatus() 255 return ( 256 257 ) 258 } 259 ``` 260 261 You can "debounce" the hint by adding an initial animation delay (e.g. 100ms) and starting as invisible (e.g. `opacity: 0`). This means the loading indicator will only be shown if the navigation takes longer than the specified delay. See the [`useLinkStatus` reference](/docs/app/api-reference/functions/use-link-status#gracefully-handling-fast-navigation) for a CSS example. 262 263 > **Good to know**: An **experimental** [`useOffline`](/docs/app/api-reference/config/next-config-js/useOffline) hook can keep prefetched routes navigable during connectivity drops. See the [offline support guide](/docs/app/guides/offline-support). 264 265 > **Good to know**: You can use other visual feedback patterns like a progress bar. View an example [here](https://github.com/vercel/react-transition-progress). 266 267 ### Disabling prefetching 268 269 You can opt out of prefetching by setting the `prefetch` prop to `false` on the `` component. This is useful to avoid unnecessary usage of resources when rendering large lists of links (e.g. an infinite scroll table). 270 271 ```tsx 272 273 Blog 274 275 ``` 276 277 However, disabling prefetching comes with trade-offs: 278 279 - **Static routes** will only be fetched when the user clicks the link. 280 - **Dynamic routes** will need to be rendered on the server first before the client can navigate to it. 281 282 To reduce resource usage without fully disabling prefetch, you can prefetch only on hover. This limits prefetching to routes the user is more _likely_ to visit, rather than all links in the viewport. 283 284 ```tsx filename="app/ui/hover-prefetch-link.tsx" switcher 285 'use client' 286 287 import Link from 'next/link' 288 import { useState } from 'react' 289 290 function HoverPrefetchLink({ 291 href, 292 children, 293 }: { 294 href: string 295 children: React.ReactNode 296 }) { 297 const [active, setActive] = useState(false) 298 299 return ( 300 setActive(true)} 304 > 305 {children} 306 307 ) 308 } 309 ``` 310 311 ```jsx filename="app/ui/hover-prefetch-link.js" switcher 312 'use client' 313 314 import Link from 'next/link' 315 import { useState } from 'react' 316 317 function HoverPrefetchLink({ href, children }) { 318 const [active, setActive] = useState(false) 319 320 return ( 321 setActive(true)} 325 > 326 {children} 327 328 ) 329 } 330 ``` 331 332 ### Hydration not completed 333 334 `` is a Client Component and must be hydrated before it can prefetch routes. On the initial visit, large JavaScript bundles can delay hydration, preventing prefetching from starting right away. 335 336 React mitigates this with Selective Hydration and you can further improve this by: 337 338 - Using the [`@next/bundle-analyzer`](/docs/app/guides/package-bundling#nextbundle-analyzer-for-webpack) plugin to identify and reduce bundle size by removing large dependencies. 339 - Moving logic from the client to the server where possible. See the [Server and Client Components](/docs/app/getting-started/server-and-client-components) docs for guidance. 340 341 ## Examples 342 343 ### Native History API 344 345 Next.js allows you to use the native [`window.history.pushState`](https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/API/History/pushState) and [`window.history.replaceState`](https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/API/History/replaceState) methods to update the browser's history stack without reloading the page. 346 347 `pushState` and `replaceState` calls integrate into the Next.js Router, allowing you to sync with [`usePathname`](/docs/app/api-reference/functions/use-pathname) and [`useSearchParams`](/docs/app/api-reference/functions/use-search-params). 348 349 #### `window.history.pushState` 350 351 Use it to add a new entry to the browser's history stack. The user can navigate back to the previous state. For example, to sort a list of products: 352 353 ```tsx fileName="app/ui/sort-products.tsx" switcher 354 'use client' 355 356 import { useSearchParams } from 'next/navigation' 357 358 export default function SortProducts() { 359 const searchParams = useSearchParams() 360 361 function updateSorting(sortOrder: string) { 362 const params = new URLSearchParams(searchParams.toString()) 363 params.set('sort', sortOrder) 364 window.history.pushState(null, '', `?${params.toString()}`) 365 } 366 367 return ( 368 <> 369 370 371 372 ) 373 } 374 ``` 375 376 ```jsx fileName="app/ui/sort-products.js" switcher 377 'use client' 378 379 import { useSearchParams } from 'next/navigation' 380 381 export default function SortProducts() { 382 const searchParams = useSearchParams() 383 384 function updateSorting(sortOrder) { 385 const params = new URLSearchParams(searchParams.toString()) 386 params.set('sort', sortOrder) 387 window.history.pushState(null, '', `?${params.toString()}`) 388 } 389 390 return ( 391 <> 392 393 394 395 ) 396 } 397 ``` 398 399 #### `window.history.replaceState` 400 401 Use it to replace the current entry on the browser's history stack. The user is not able to navigate back to the previous state. For example, to switch the application's locale: 402 403 ```tsx fileName="app/ui/locale-switcher.tsx" switcher 404 'use client' 405 406 import { usePathname } from 'next/navigation' 407 408 export function LocaleSwitcher() { 409 const pathname = usePathname() 410 411 function switchLocale(locale: string) { 412 // e.g. '/en/about' or '/fr/contact' 413 const newPath = `/${locale}${pathname}` 414 window.history.replaceState(null, '', newPath) 415 } 416 417 return ( 418 <> 419 420 421 422 ) 423 } 424 ``` 425 426 ```jsx fileName="app/ui/locale-switcher.js" switcher 427 'use client' 428 429 import { usePathname } from 'next/navigation' 430 431 export function LocaleSwitcher() { 432 const pathname = usePathname() 433 434 function switchLocale(locale) { 435 // e.g. '/en/about' or '/fr/contact' 436 const newPath = `/${locale}${pathname}` 437 window.history.replaceState(null, '', newPath) 438 } 439 440 return ( 441 <> 442 443 444 445 ) 446 } 447 ``` 448

See [`devIndicators`](/docs/app/api-reference/config/next-config-js/devIndicators) for more information. 188 189 ### Dynamic segments without `generateStaticParams` 190 191 If a [dynamic segment](/docs/app/api-reference/file-conventions/dynamic-routes) could be prerendered but isn't because it's missing [`generateStaticParams`](/docs/app/api-reference/functions/generate-static-params), the route will fallback to dynamic rendering at request time. 192 193 Ensure the route is statically generated at build time by adding `generateStaticParams`: 194 195 ```tsx filename="app/blog/[slug]/page.tsx" switcher 196 export async function generateStaticParams() { 197 const posts = await fetch('https://.../posts').then((res) => res.json()) 198 199 return posts.map((post) => ({ 200 slug: post.slug, 201 })) 202 } 203 204 export default async function Page({ 205 params, 206 }: { 207 params: Promise<{ slug: string }> 208 }) { 209 const { slug } = await params 210 // ... 211 } 212 ``` 213 214 ```jsx filename="app/blog/[slug]/page.js" switcher 215 export async function generateStaticParams() { 216 const posts = await fetch('https://.../posts').then((res) => res.json()) 217 218 return posts.map((post) => ({ 219 slug: post.slug, 220 })) 221 } 222 223 export default async function Page({ params }) { 224 const { slug } = await params 225 // ... 226 } 227 ``` 228 229 ### Slow networks 230 231 On slow or unstable networks, prefetching may not finish before the user clicks a link. This can affect both static and dynamic routes. In these cases, the `loading.js` fallback may not appear immediately because it hasn't been prefetched yet. 232 233 To improve perceived performance, you can use the [`useLinkStatus` hook](/docs/app/api-reference/functions/use-link-status) to show immediate feedback while the transition is in progress. 234 235 ```tsx filename="app/ui/loading-indicator.tsx" switcher 236 'use client' 237 238 import { useLinkStatus } from 'next/link' 239 240 export default function LoadingIndicator() { 241 const { pending } = useLinkStatus() 242 return ( 243 244 ) 245 } 246 ``` 247 248 ```jsx filename="app/ui/loading-indicator.js" switcher 249 'use client' 250 251 import { useLinkStatus } from 'next/link' 252 253 export default function LoadingIndicator() { 254 const { pending } = useLinkStatus() 255 return ( 256 257 ) 258 } 259 ``` 260 261 You can "debounce" the hint by adding an initial animation delay (e.g. 100ms) and starting as invisible (e.g. `opacity: 0`). This means the loading indicator will only be shown if the navigation takes longer than the specified delay. See the [`useLinkStatus` reference](/docs/app/api-reference/functions/use-link-status#gracefully-handling-fast-navigation) for a CSS example. 262 263 > **Good to know**: An **experimental** [`useOffline`](/docs/app/api-reference/config/next-config-js/useOffline) hook can keep prefetched routes navigable during connectivity drops. See the [offline support guide](/docs/app/guides/offline-support). 264 265 > **Good to know**: You can use other visual feedback patterns like a progress bar. View an example [here](https://github.com/vercel/react-transition-progress). 266 267 ### Disabling prefetching 268 269 You can opt out of prefetching by setting the `prefetch` prop to `false` on the `` component. This is useful to avoid unnecessary usage of resources when rendering large lists of links (e.g. an infinite scroll table). 270 271 ```tsx 272 273 Blog 274 275 ``` 276 277 However, disabling prefetching comes with trade-offs: 278 279 - **Static routes** will only be fetched when the user clicks the link. 280 - **Dynamic routes** will need to be rendered on the server first before the client can navigate to it. 281 282 To reduce resource usage without fully disabling prefetch, you can prefetch only on hover. This limits prefetching to routes the user is more _likely_ to visit, rather than all links in the viewport. 283 284 ```tsx filename="app/ui/hover-prefetch-link.tsx" switcher 285 'use client' 286 287 import Link from 'next/link' 288 import { useState } from 'react' 289 290 function HoverPrefetchLink({ 291 href, 292 children, 293 }: { 294 href: string 295 children: React.ReactNode 296 }) { 297 const [active, setActive] = useState(false) 298 299 return ( 300 setActive(true)} 304 > 305 {children} 306 307 ) 308 } 309 ``` 310 311 ```jsx filename="app/ui/hover-prefetch-link.js" switcher 312 'use client' 313 314 import Link from 'next/link' 315 import { useState } from 'react' 316 317 function HoverPrefetchLink({ href, children }) { 318 const [active, setActive] = useState(false) 319 320 return ( 321 setActive(true)} 325 > 326 {children} 327 328 ) 329 } 330 ``` 331 332 ### Hydration not completed 333 334 `` is a Client Component and must be hydrated before it can prefetch routes. On the initial visit, large JavaScript bundles can delay hydration, preventing prefetching from starting right away. 335 336 React mitigates this with Selective Hydration and you can further improve this by: 337 338 - Using the [`@next/bundle-analyzer`](/docs/app/guides/package-bundling#nextbundle-analyzer-for-webpack) plugin to identify and reduce bundle size by removing large dependencies. 339 - Moving logic from the client to the server where possible. See the [Server and Client Components](/docs/app/getting-started/server-and-client-components) docs for guidance. 340 341 ## Examples 342 343 ### Native History API 344 345 Next.js allows you to use the native [`window.history.pushState`](https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/API/History/pushState) and [`window.history.replaceState`](https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/API/History/replaceState) methods to update the browser's history stack without reloading the page. 346 347 `pushState` and `replaceState` calls integrate into the Next.js Router, allowing you to sync with [`usePathname`](/docs/app/api-reference/functions/use-pathname) and [`useSearchParams`](/docs/app/api-reference/functions/use-search-params). 348 349 #### `window.history.pushState` 350 351 Use it to add a new entry to the browser's history stack. The user can navigate back to the previous state. For example, to sort a list of products: 352 353 ```tsx fileName="app/ui/sort-products.tsx" switcher 354 'use client' 355 356 import { useSearchParams } from 'next/navigation' 357 358 export default function SortProducts() { 359 const searchParams = useSearchParams() 360 361 function updateSorting(sortOrder: string) { 362 const params = new URLSearchParams(searchParams.toString()) 363 params.set('sort', sortOrder) 364 window.history.pushState(null, '', `?${params.toString()}`) 365 } 366 367 return ( 368 <> 369 370 371 372 ) 373 } 374 ``` 375 376 ```jsx fileName="app/ui/sort-products.js" switcher 377 'use client' 378 379 import { useSearchParams } from 'next/navigation' 380 381 export default function SortProducts() { 382 const searchParams = useSearchParams() 383 384 function updateSorting(sortOrder) { 385 const params = new URLSearchParams(searchParams.toString()) 386 params.set('sort', sortOrder) 387 window.history.pushState(null, '', `?${params.toString()}`) 388 } 389 390 return ( 391 <> 392 393 394 395 ) 396 } 397 ``` 398 399 #### `window.history.replaceState` 400 401 Use it to replace the current entry on the browser's history stack. The user is not able to navigate back to the previous state. For example, to switch the application's locale: 402 403 ```tsx fileName="app/ui/locale-switcher.tsx" switcher 404 'use client' 405 406 import { usePathname } from 'next/navigation' 407 408 export function LocaleSwitcher() { 409 const pathname = usePathname() 410 411 function switchLocale(locale: string) { 412 // e.g. '/en/about' or '/fr/contact' 413 const newPath = `/${locale}${pathname}` 414 window.history.replaceState(null, '', newPath) 415 } 416 417 return ( 418 <> 419 420 421 422 ) 423 } 424 ``` 425 426 ```jsx fileName="app/ui/locale-switcher.js" switcher 427 'use client' 428 429 import { usePathname } from 'next/navigation' 430 431 export function LocaleSwitcher() { 432 const pathname = usePathname() 433 434 function switchLocale(locale) { 435 // e.g. '/en/about' or '/fr/contact' 436 const newPath = `/${locale}${pathname}` 437 window.history.replaceState(null, '', newPath) 438 } 439 440 return ( 441 <> 442 443 444 445 ) 446 } 447 ``` 448

title: Link Component
description: Enable fast client-side navigation with the built-in `next/link` component.
---

{/* The content of this doc is shared between the app and pages router. You can use the `<PagesOnly>Content</PagesOnly>` component to add content that is specific to the Pages Router. Any shared content should not be wrapped in a component. */}

`<Link>` is a React component that extends the HTML `<a>` element to provide [prefetching](/docs/app/getting-started/linking-and-navigating#prefetching) and client-side navigation between routes. It is the primary way to navigate between routes in Next.js.

Basic usage:

<AppOnly>

```tsx filename="app/page.tsx" switcher
import Link from 'next/link'

export default function Page() {
  return <Link href="/dashboard">Dashboard</Link>
}
```

```jsx filename="app/page.js" switcher
import Link from 'next/link'

export default function Page() {
  return <Link href="/dashboard">Dashboard</Link>
}
```

</AppOnly>

<PagesOnly>

```tsx filename="pages/index.tsx" switcher
import Link from 'next/link'

export default function Home() {
  return <Link href="/dashboard">Dashboard</Link>
}
```

```jsx filename="pages/index.js" switcher
import Link from 'next/link'

export default function Home() {
  return <Link href="/dashboard">Dashboard</Link>
}
```

</PagesOnly>

## Reference

The following props can be passed to the `<Link>` component:

<PagesOnly>

| Prop                        | Example                  | Type              | Required |

| [`href`](#href-required)    | `href="/dashboard"`      | String or Object  | Yes      |

| [`onNavigate`](#onnavigate) | `onNavigate={(e) => {}}` | Function          | -        |

| [`replace`](#replace)                 | `replace={false}`                | Boolean          | -        |
